extracted.intended_audience: funding agencies, academic institutions, publishers, organizations that supply metrics, and individual researchers (research-assessment stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA): a set of recommended practices for assessing the quality and impact of research outputs, addressing funders, institutions, publishers, metric-providers, and researchers. Focuses on moving assessment away from journal-based metrics toward article- and output-level, transparent, and qualitative measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use journal-based metrics as surrogate measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use journal-based metrics, such as Journal Impact Factors, as a surrogate measure of the quality of individual research articles, to assess an individual scientist’s contributions, or in hiring, promotion, or funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Recommendation: The Journal Impact Factor was created as a tool to help librarians identify journals to purchase, not as a measure of the scientific quality of research in an article. Use of journal-based metrics in individual assessment is discouraged because citation distributions are skewed, metrics are field-specific, can be manipulated, and their underlying data are not transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding agencies: be explicit about evaluation criteria; emphasize content
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the criteria used in evaluating the scientific productivity of grant applicants and clearly highlight, especially for early-stage investigators, that the scientific content of a paper is much more important than publication metrics or the identity of the journal in which it was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding agencies should make criteria transparent and communicate that scientific content matters more than where a paper is published; this is especially important for early-stage investigators to ensure fair assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding agencies: consider all research outputs and broad impact measures
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of research assessment, consider the value and impact of all research outputs (including datasets and software) in addition to research publications, and consider a broad range of impact measures including qualitative indicators of research impact, such as influence on policy and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages funders to evaluate diverse outputs (data, software, reagents, IP, trained researchers) and to use both quantitative and qualitative indicators (e.g., policy influence) rather than relying solely on publication metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions: be explicit about hiring/tenure/promotion criteria; emphasize content
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the criteria used to reach hiring, tenure, and promotion decisions, clearly highlighting, especially for early-stage investigators, that the scientific content of a paper is much more important than publication metrics or the identity of the journal in which it was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities and research institutions should publicly state evaluation criteria and prioritize scientific merit of outputs over journal reputation, supporting fair assessment of early-career researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions: consider all research outputs and broad impact measures
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of research assessment, consider the value and impact of all research outputs (including datasets and software) in addition to research publications, and consider a broad range of impact measures including qualitative indicators of research impact, such as influence on policy and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional assessment should recognize and reward diverse scholarly contributions (datasets, software, trained scientists, etc.) and include qualitative impacts (e.g., practice or policy changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers: reduce emphasis on journal impact factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatly reduce emphasis on the journal impact factor as a promotional tool, ideally by ceasing to promote the impact factor or by presenting the metric in the context of a variety of journal-based metrics (e.g., 5-year impact factor, EigenFactor, SCImago, h-index, editorial and publication times, etc.) that provide a richer view of journal performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should stop using JIF as primary promotional metric and, if presenting it, contextualize it alongside multiple other journal-level indicators to give a fuller picture of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers: provide article-level metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Make available a range of article-level metrics to encourage a shift toward assessment based on the scientific content of an article rather than publication metrics of the journal in which it was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article-level indicators (citations, usage, altmetrics, etc.) should be accessible so assessment can focus on the specific article's influence instead of the journal's aggregate metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers: encourage responsible authorship and declare contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage responsible authorship practices and the provision of information about the specific contributions of each author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should require or encourage clear statements of author contribution to improve accountability and appropriately allocate credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers: remove reuse limitations on reference lists (CC0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a journal is open-access or subscription-based, remove all reuse limitations on reference lists in research articles and make them available under the Creative Commons Public Domain Dedication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference lists should be openly reusable (e.g., CC0) to support transparency, bibliometrics, and broader reuse of citation data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers: relax reference limits; prefer primary literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove or reduce the constraints on the number of references in research articles, and, where appropriate, mandate the citation of primary literature in favor of reviews in order to give credit to the group(s) who first reported a finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations on references can distort credit; journals should allow sufficient referencing and favor citing original reports to properly credit original work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric providers: be open and transparent about data and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Be open and transparent by providing data and methods used to calculate all metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppliers of bibliometric and other metrics must publish the underlying data and computational methods to allow scrutiny, reproducibility, and informed use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric providers: provide data under an unrestricted licence and computational access
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the data under a licence that allows unrestricted reuse, and provide computational access to data, where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open licensing and programmatic access enable independent analysis, validation, and broader uses of metric datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric providers: define and act against inappropriate manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear that inappropriate manipulation of metrics will not be tolerated; be explicit about what constitutes inappropriate manipulation and what measures will be taken to combat this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providers should state definitions of gaming/manipulation and the sanctions or corrective measures they will apply to preserve metric integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric providers: account for variation in article types and fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the variation in article types (e.g., reviews versus research articles), and in different subject areas when metrics are used, aggregated, or compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons using metrics must normalize or otherwise adjust for differences across article types and disciplines to avoid misleading evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researchers on committees: assess based on scientific content
rubrics_metrics.description: When involved in committees making decisions about funding, hiring, tenure, or promotion, make assessments based on scientific content rather than publication metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers who evaluate peers should prioritize reading and evaluating the actual work and its merits, not relying on journal-level indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researchers: cite primary literature where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever appropriate, cite primary literature in which observations are first reported rather than reviews in order to give credit where credit is due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing original reports ensures credit accrues to the researchers who first made findings, rather than to secondary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researchers: use a range of article metrics and indicators in statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a range of article metrics and indicators on personal/supporting statements, as evidence of the impact of individual published articles and other research outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals should present multiple indicators (quantitative and qualitative) to document the influence of their outputs rather than relying on journal titles or impact factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researchers: challenge inappropriate assessment practices and teach best practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenge research assessment practices that rely inappropriately on Journal Impact Factors and promote and teach best practice that focuses on the value and influence of specific research outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should advocate for improved assessment approaches within their communities and mentor others about fair evaluation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the Journal Impact Factor (JIF)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Journal Impact Factor has a number of well-documented deficiencies as a tool for research assessment. These limitations include: A) citation distributions within journals are highly skewed; B) the properties of the Journal Impact Factor are field-specific: it is a composite of multiple, highly diverse article types, including primary research papers and reviews; C) Journal Impact Factors can be manipulated (or “gamed”) by editorial policy; and D) data used to calculate the Journal Impact Factors are neither transparent nor openly available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of skewed citation distributions, field-specificity, potential for editorial manipulation, and lack of transparency in underlying data, JIF is unsuitable as a primary measure of individual article or researcher quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize diverse research outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: The outputs from scientific research are many and varied, including: research articles reporting new knowledge, data, reagents, and software; intellectual property; and highly trained young scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment frameworks should recognize and value a broad set of outputs beyond peer-reviewed articles (datasets, software, reagents, IP, trained researchers) when evaluating research effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overarching themes of the Declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of themes run through these recommendations: the need to eliminate the use of journal-based metrics, such as Journal Impact Factors, in funding, appointment, and promotion considerations; the need to assess research on its own merits rather than on the basis of the journal in which the research is published; and the need to capitalize on the opportunities provided by online publication (such as relaxing unnecessary limits on the number of words, figures, and references in articles, and exploring new indicators of significance and impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three cross-cutting principles should guide policy changes across funders, institutions, publishers, metric-providers, and researchers to move toward more meaningful and fair research assessment practices.
